CHAPTER XXI.
A RECOGNITION


Nothing occurred in the night to flutter the tired dove; and the dove
arose refreshed. With Mr. Grewgious, when the clock struck ten in the
morning, came Mr. Crisparkle, who had come at one plunge out of the
river at Cloisterham.

“Miss Twinkleton was so uneasy, Miss Rosa,” he explained to her, “and
came round to Ma and me with your note, in such a state of wonder,
that, to quiet her, I volunteered on this service by the very first
train to be caught in the morning. I wished at the time that you had
come to me; but now I think it best that you did _as_ you did, and came
to your guardian.”

“I did think of you,” Rosa told him; “but Minor Canon Corner was so
near him—”

“I understand. It was quite natural.”

“I have told Mr. Crisparkle,” said Mr. Grewgious, “all that you told me
last night, my dear. Of course I should have written it to him
immediately; but his coming was most opportune. And it was particularly
kind of him to come, for he had but just gone.”

“Have you settled,” asked Rosa, appealing to them both, “what is to be
done for Helena and her brother?”

“Why really,” said Mr. Crisparkle, “I am in great perplexity. If even
Mr. Grewgious, whose head is much longer than mine, and who is a whole
night’s cogitation in advance of me, is undecided, what must I be!”

The Unlimited here put her head in at the door—after having rapped, and
been authorised to present herself—announcing that a gentleman wished
for a word with another gentleman named Crisparkle, if any such
gentleman were there. If no such gentleman were there, he begged pardon
for being mistaken.

“Such a gentleman is here,” said Mr. Crisparkle, “but is engaged just
now.”

“Is it a dark gentleman?” interposed Rosa, retreating on her guardian.

“No, Miss, more of a brown gentleman.”

“You are sure not with black hair?” asked Rosa, taking courage.

“Quite sure of that, Miss. Brown hair and blue eyes.”

“Perhaps,” hinted Mr. Grewgious, with habitual caution, “it might be
well to see him, reverend sir, if you don’t object. When one is in a
difficulty or at a loss, one never knows in what direction a way out
may chance to open. It is a business principle of mine, in such a case,
not to close up any direction, but to keep an eye on every direction
that may present itself. I could relate an anecdote in point, but that
it would be premature.”

“If Miss Rosa will allow me, then? Let the gentleman come in,” said Mr.
Crisparkle.

The gentleman came in; apologised, with a frank but modest grace, for
not finding Mr. Crisparkle alone; turned to Mr. Crisparkle, and
smilingly asked the unexpected question: “Who am I?”

“You are the gentleman I saw smoking under the trees in Staple Inn, a
few minutes ago.”

“True. There I saw you. Who else am I?”

Mr. Crisparkle concentrated his attention on a handsome face, much
sunburnt; and the ghost of some departed boy seemed to rise, gradually
and dimly, in the room.

The gentleman saw a struggling recollection lighten up the Minor
Canon’s features, and smiling again, said: “What will you have for
breakfast this morning? You are out of jam.”

“Wait a moment!” cried Mr. Crisparkle, raising his right hand. “Give me
another instant! Tartar!”

The two shook hands with the greatest heartiness, and then went the
wonderful length—for Englishmen—of laying their hands each on the
other’s shoulders, and looking joyfully each into the other’s face.

“My old fag!” said Mr. Crisparkle.

“My old master!” said Mr. Tartar.

“You saved me from drowning!” said Mr. Crisparkle.

“After which you took to swimming, you know!” said Mr. Tartar.

“God bless my soul!” said Mr. Crisparkle.

“Amen!” said Mr. Tartar.

And then they fell to shaking hands most heartily again.

“Imagine,” exclaimed Mr. Crisparkle, with glistening eyes: “Miss Rosa
Bud and Mr. Grewgious, imagine Mr. Tartar, when he was the smallest of
juniors, diving for me, catching me, a big heavy senior, by the hair of
the head, and striking out for the shore with me like a water-giant!”

“Imagine my not letting him sink, as I was his fag!” said Mr. Tartar.
“But the truth being that he was my best protector and friend, and did
me more good than all the masters put together, an irrational impulse
seized me to pick him up, or go down with him.”

“Hem! Permit me, sir, to have the honour,” said Mr. Grewgious,
advancing with extended hand, “for an honour I truly esteem it. I am
proud to make your acquaintance. I hope you didn’t take cold. I hope
you were not inconvenienced by swallowing too much water. How have you
been since?”

It was by no means apparent that Mr. Grewgious knew what he said,
though it was very apparent that he meant to say something highly
friendly and appreciative.

If Heaven, Rosa thought, had but sent such courage and skill to her
poor mother’s aid! And he to have been so slight and young then!

“I don’t wish to be complimented upon it, I thank you; but I think I
have an idea,” Mr. Grewgious announced, after taking a jog-trot or two
across the room, so unexpected and unaccountable that they all stared
at him, doubtful whether he was choking or had the cramp—“I _think_ I
have an idea. I believe I have had the pleasure of seeing Mr. Tartar’s
name as tenant of the top set in the house next the top set in the
corner?”

“Yes, sir,” returned Mr. Tartar. “You are right so far.”

“I am right so far,” said Mr. Grewgious. “Tick that off;” which he did,
with his right thumb on his left. “Might you happen to know the name of
your neighbour in the top set on the other side of the party-wall?”
coming very close to Mr. Tartar, to lose nothing of his face, in his
shortness of sight.

“Landless.”

“Tick that off,” said Mr. Grewgious, taking another trot, and then
coming back. “No personal knowledge, I suppose, sir?”

“Slight, but some.”

“Tick that off,” said Mr. Grewgious, taking another trot, and again
coming back. “Nature of knowledge, Mr. Tartar?”

“I thought he seemed to be a young fellow in a poor way, and I asked
his leave—only within a day or so—to share my flowers up there with
him; that is to say, to extend my flower-garden to his windows.”

“Would you have the kindness to take seats?” said Mr. Grewgious. “I
_have_ an idea!”

They complied; Mr. Tartar none the less readily, for being all abroad;
and Mr. Grewgious, seated in the centre, with his hands upon his knees,
thus stated his idea, with his usual manner of having got the statement
by heart.

“I cannot as yet make up my mind whether it is prudent to hold open
communication under present circumstances, and on the part of the fair
member of the present company, with Mr. Neville or Miss Helena. I have
reason to know that a local friend of ours (on whom I beg to bestow a
passing but a hearty malediction, with the kind permission of my
reverend friend) sneaks to and fro, and dodges up and down. When not
doing so himself, he may have some informant skulking about, in the
person of a watchman, porter, or such-like hanger-on of Staple. On the
other hand, Miss Rosa very naturally wishes to see her friend Miss
Helena, and it would seem important that at least Miss Helena (if not
her brother too, through her) should privately know from Miss Rosa’s
lips what has occurred, and what has been threatened. Am I agreed with
generally in the views I take?”

“I entirely coincide with them,” said Mr. Crisparkle, who had been very
attentive.

“As I have no doubt I should,” added Mr. Tartar, smiling, “if I
understood them.”

“Fair and softly, sir,” said Mr. Grewgious; “we shall fully confide in
you directly, if you will favour us with your permission. Now, if our
local friend should have any informant on the spot, it is tolerably
clear that such informant can only be set to watch the chambers in the
occupation of Mr. Neville. He reporting, to our local friend, who comes
and goes there, our local friend would supply for himself, from his own
previous knowledge, the identity of the parties. Nobody can be set to
watch all Staple, or to concern himself with comers and goers to other
sets of chambers: unless, indeed, mine.”

“I begin to understand to what you tend,” said Mr. Crisparkle, “and
highly approve of your caution.”

“I needn’t repeat that I know nothing yet of the why and wherefore,”
said Mr. Tartar; “but I also understand to what you tend, so let me say
at once that my chambers are freely at your disposal.”

“There!” cried Mr. Grewgious, smoothing his head triumphantly, “now we
have all got the idea. You have it, my dear?”

“I think I have,” said Rosa, blushing a little as Mr. Tartar looked
quickly towards her.

“You see, you go over to Staple with Mr. Crisparkle and Mr. Tartar,”
said Mr. Grewgious; “I going in and out, and out and in alone, in my
usual way; you go up with those gentlemen to Mr. Tartar’s rooms; you
look into Mr. Tartar’s flower-garden; you wait for Miss Helena’s
appearance there, or you signify to Miss Helena that you are close by;
and you communicate with her freely, and no spy can be the wiser.”

“I am very much afraid I shall be—”

“Be what, my dear?” asked Mr. Grewgious, as she hesitated. “Not
frightened?”

“No, not that,” said Rosa, shyly; “in Mr. Tartar’s way. We seem to be
appropriating Mr. Tartar’s residence so very coolly.”

“I protest to you,” returned that gentleman, “that I shall think the
better of it for evermore, if your voice sounds in it only once.”

Rosa, not quite knowing what to say about that, cast down her eyes, and
turning to Mr. Grewgious, dutifully asked if she should put her hat on?
Mr. Grewgious being of opinion that she could not do better, she
withdrew for the purpose. Mr. Crisparkle took the opportunity of giving
Mr. Tartar a summary of the distresses of Neville and his sister; the
opportunity was quite long enough, as the hat happened to require a
little extra fitting on.

Mr. Tartar gave his arm to Rosa, and Mr. Crisparkle walked, detached,
in front.

“Poor, poor Eddy!” thought Rosa, as they went along.

Mr. Tartar waved his right hand as he bent his head down over Rosa,
talking in an animated way.

“It was not so powerful or so sun-browned when it saved Mr.
Crisparkle,” thought Rosa, glancing at it; “but it must have been very
steady and determined even then.”

Mr. Tartar told her he had been a sailor, roving everywhere for years
and years.

“When are you going to sea again?” asked Rosa.

“Never!”

Rosa wondered what the girls would say if they could see her crossing
the wide street on the sailor’s arm. And she fancied that the
passers-by must think her very little and very helpless, contrasted
with the strong figure that could have caught her up and carried her
out of any danger, miles and miles without resting.

She was thinking further, that his far-seeing blue eyes looked as if
they had been used to watch danger afar off, and to watch it without
flinching, drawing nearer and nearer: when, happening to raise her own
eyes, she found that he seemed to be thinking something about _them_.

This a little confused Rosebud, and may account for her never
afterwards quite knowing how she ascended (with his help) to his garden
in the air, and seemed to get into a marvellous country that came into
sudden bloom like the country on the summit of the magic bean-stalk.
May it flourish for ever!

The night passed quietly, undisturbed by any alarm or unease—like a bird resting in peace, the weary soul awoke refreshed. At ten o’clock sharp, Mr. Grewgious arrived, accompanied by Mr. Crisparkle, who had made the journey from Cloisterham without delay, arriving straight from the river’s edge.

“Miss Twinkleton was so anxious,” Mr. Crisparkle explained to Rosa, “that she came rushing over to my mother and me with your note, all agitated and bewildered. To calm her, I offered to come at once—the very first train of the morning. I confess I wished you had turned to me first, but now I see that your choice was wise: coming to your guardian was the right course.”

“I did consider you,” Rosa replied, “but Minor Canon Corner was so close to him—”

“I understand perfectly,” said Mr. Crisparkle. “It was entirely natural.”

“I’ve already told Mr. Crisparkle everything you shared with me last night,” Mr. Grewgious added gently. “Of course, I would have written to him immediately—but his arrival could not have been more timely. And it was most thoughtful of him to come, especially since he’d only just left.”

Rosa turned to both men, her voice filled with concern. “Have you decided what should be done for Helena and her brother?”

“Honestly,” Mr. Crisparkle admitted, “I’m at a loss. If even Mr. Grewgious, whose mind is far more seasoned than mine, cannot settle on a plan after a full night of thought, then what hope do I have?”

Just then, the Unlimited appeared at the door—having knocked and received permission to enter—announcing a gentleman who wished to speak briefly with someone named Crisparkle, if such a person were present. Should no such man be there, he apologized for the mistake.

“There is such a gentleman,” Mr. Crisparkle said, “but he’s occupied just now.”

“Is it a dark gentleman?” Rosa asked, stepping back toward her guardian.

“No, miss,” the servant replied. “More of a brown gentleman.”

“You’re certain he doesn’t have black hair?” Rosa pressed, gaining courage.

“Quite sure, miss. Brown hair and blue eyes.”

Mr. Grewgious paused, his usual caution surfacing. “Perhaps, reverend sir, it might be prudent to meet him—if you don’t object. When one is uncertain, one never knows where help might appear. It’s a principle I follow: keep every avenue open. I could tell a story to illustrate, but that would be premature.”

“If Miss Rosa will allow it,” Mr. Crisparkle said, “let the gentleman come in.”

The visitor entered, politely apologizing for interrupting. With a modest yet sincere grace, he turned to Mr. Crisparkle and smiled. Then, with an unexpected twist, he asked: “Who am I?”

“You are the gentleman I saw smoking beneath the trees in Staple Inn just moments ago,” Mr. Crisparkle replied.

“True,” the man acknowledged. “And there, I saw you. But who else am I?”

Mr. Crisparkle studied the handsome, sun-bronzed face before him. Slowly, a memory stirred—a ghost of a younger boy rising faintly in the room. The man noticed the flicker of recognition and smiled again.

“What shall we have for breakfast this morning?” he asked lightly. “You’re out of jam.”

“Wait!” Mr. Crisparkle exclaimed, raising his hand. “One moment! Tartar!”

They embraced warmly, their hands clasping tightly, then each placing a hand on the other’s shoulder, gazing into one another’s eyes with unmistakable joy.

“My old fag!” Mr. Crisparkle declared.
“My old master!” the other replied.
“You saved me from drowning!”
“And afterward, you took to swimming, didn’t you?”
“God bless my soul!”
“Amen!”

They shook hands again, heartily, as if sealing a bond long overdue.

“Imagine,” Mr. Crisparkle said, eyes shining, “Miss Rosa Bud and Mr. Grewgious—imagine Mr. Tartar, when he was barely a junior, diving into the water to save me, a heavy senior, grabbing me by the hair, and swimming like a water-giant toward shore!”

“And imagine me refusing to let him sink,” Mr. Tartar added, “even though I was his fag. But the truth is—he was my greatest protector, my truest friend. He did me more good than all the masters combined. So when I saw him struggling, an instinct took hold: either I save him—or go down with him.”

“Hem!” Mr. Grewgious interjected, stepping forward with extended hand. “Permit me the honor—for it is truly an honor. I am proud to make your acquaintance. I hope you didn’t catch cold. I hope the water didn’t trouble you. How have you been since?”

His words seemed unformed, as if spoken without full awareness, though clearly meant to convey warmth and respect. Rosa watched, thinking: *If Heaven had sent such courage and strength to my poor mother!* And to think—this man had once been so slight, so young.

“I don’t wish to be praised,” Mr. Tartar said humbly, “but I believe I have an idea.”

He began pacing across the room in a sudden, almost erratic manner—so unusual that everyone stared, wondering if he were choking or seized by cramp.

“I _think_,” he announced, “I believe I’ve had the pleasure of seeing Mr. Tartar’s name listed as tenant of the top set in the house next to the corner one?”

“Yes, sir,” Mr. Tartar replied. “You’re correct so far.”

“Tick that off,” Mr. Grewgious said, tapping his thumb against his palm. “Now, might you know the name of your neighbor in the top set on the other side of the party wall?” He leaned close, his short sight demanding proximity.

“Landless.”

“Tick that off,” Mr. Grewgious said, taking another quick step, then returning. “No personal knowledge, I suppose?”

“Only slight—but some.”

“Tick that off,” he repeated, pacing again. “Nature of your knowledge, Mr. Tartar?”

“I thought he looked like a young man in difficult circumstances. Only recently—within a day or two—I asked his permission to extend my flower garden to his windows—that is, to share my blooms with him.”

“Would you kindly take seats?” Mr. Grewgious requested. “I _have_ an idea.”

They sat. Mr. Tartar complied readily, despite seeming slightly disoriented. Mr. Grewgious, seated in the center, hands resting on his knees, spoke with his customary precision—though it was clear he’d rehearsed the words.

“I cannot yet decide whether it’s safe to maintain contact, under current conditions, between the fair member of this company and Mr. Neville or Miss Helena. I know a local associate of ours—on whom I beg to bestow a passing, but heartfelt, curse, with the kind indulgence of my reverend friend—moves stealthily, skulking about. He may have an informant: a watchman, porter, or some other lowly figure attached to Staple. If not himself, he might have planted someone to monitor Mr. Neville’s chambers. That person would report to our friend, who would then deduce identities from prior knowledge. But no one can watch every chamber, nor track every visitor—unless, perhaps, mine.”

“I begin to grasp your meaning,” Mr. Crisparkle said, nodding. “And I fully approve of your caution.”

“I know nothing yet of the reason or motive,” Mr. Tartar said, “but I understand your intent. Let me say plainly: my rooms are yours to use.”

“There!” Mr. Grewgious declared, smoothing his head with triumph. “Now we all have the idea. Do you understand, my dear?”

“I think so,” Rosa replied, blushing slightly as Mr. Tartar glanced toward her.

“You’ll go to Staple with Mr. Crisparkle and Mr. Tartar,” Mr. Grewgious explained. “I’ll move in and out alone, as usual. You’ll go up to Mr. Tartar’s rooms, inspect his flower garden, wait for Miss Helena’s appearance, or signal her that you’re nearby—and communicate freely. No spy will suspect a thing.”

“I’m afraid I’ll be—” Rosa began.

“Be what, my dear?” Mr. Grewgious asked gently.

“Not frightened,” she answered shyly. “But… in Mr. Tartar’s way. We seem to be borrowing his home so casually.”

“I assure you,” Mr. Tartar said warmly, “if your voice echoes in those rooms—even once—I shall always count it a blessing.”

Rosa, unsure how to respond, lowered her eyes and turned to Mr. Grewgious. “Shall I put on my hat?”

“Nothing better you could do,” he replied. She withdrew to prepare.

While she was gone, Mr. Crisparkle gave Mr. Tartar a brief account of Neville’s troubles and Helena’s plight—the time sufficient, as the hat required careful adjustment.

When they returned, Mr. Tartar offered Rosa his arm. Mr. Crisparkle walked ahead, separate, leading the way.

“Poor, poor Eddy,” Rosa thought as they moved along.

Mr. Tartar waved his right hand, leaning down to speak animatedly. Rosa glanced at it—once so small, so pale, yet now strong and weathered. *It must have been steady and fearless even then,* she mused.

He told her he had been a sailor, roaming the seas for years.

“When are you going back?” she asked.

“Never,” he said.

Rosa wondered what the girls would think if they could see her crossing the wide street on the arm of a sailor. She imagined passers-by seeing her—small, delicate—beside this powerful figure, capable of lifting her from danger, carrying her miles without rest. His blue eyes, she noted, seemed used to watching threats approach from afar, meeting them without flinching.

Then, lifting her own gaze, she realized he was looking at her—thinking something about *her*.

A flush rose in her cheeks. Perhaps it explains why, later, she couldn’t quite remember how she climbed (with his help) to his rooftop garden, or how it felt like stepping into a magical land—suddenly blooming, like the country atop the enchanted beanstalk.

May it flourish forever.
